newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK democrats call thousands to Tiananmen protests.
newsitem.headline: HK democrats call thousands to Tiananmen protests.

text.p: Hong Kong democracy groups summoned thousands of protesters on Wednesday to honour students killed in China's 1989 military crackdown in Tiananmen Square.
Casting a shadow over Hong Kong's July 1 return to China, democrats here have rallied since Sunday against the massacre by Chinese troops of unarmed young compatriots in Beijing eight years ago.
Tens of thousands of demonstrators are expected at the principal event, an annual candlelit vigil, arranged this year around a "Pillar of Shame" statue.
Activists placed full-page newspaper advertisements urging their supporters to turn out in force to remember June 4, 1989, amid fears that China will declare future protests taboo.
In a park named after Britain's 19th century empress, Queeen Victoria, a towering grey statue of twisted human bodies depicting oppression stood in a rainstorm.
The "Pillar of Shame" will be a focus of the main evening rally, set to get under way at 20000 local time (12000 GMT).

As authorities over the border in China enforced a tight security clampdown to avert any anniversary protests, Hong Kong organisers said they expected up to 40,000 people to attend the candlelit mourning vigil on the eighth anniversary.
This is likely to be the last big pro-democracy protest in Hong Kong before Britain hands the colony of 6.4 million mostly-Chinese people to communist-ruled China in 27 days time.
The rally will demand a reversal of China's "counter- revolutionary" label on the crushed 1989 movement and the release of political prisoners in the country.

Chinese dissidents in exile including 1989 free trade union leader Han Dongfang, who lives in Hong Kong, planned to attend the rallies, although it was unclear if exiled student leaders such as Wuerkaixi would fly in for the event.

Sympathisers laid wreaths in the park in the morning to honour the "martyrs", many of them students, who died when People's Liberation Army (PLA) troops and tanks stormed Beijing's Tiananmen Square eight years ago.
Advance PLA units have already arrived in Hong Kong to establish a military garrison when China retakes control.

Students at Hong Kong University displayed anti-communist banners and paintings of the "Goddess of Democracy," icon of the doomed 1989 movement, and they planned a "Tiananmen rally" on their campus before the night-time vigil.
Advertisements in papers such as the popular Ming Pao urged Hong Kong never to forget victims of China's crackdown and the crusade of the Beijing students for democracy and clean government.
Hundreds, possibly thousands, were killed. China says tough action was needed to end a counter-revolutionary rebellion sparked by student protests.
"Never forget the June 4 massacre, never abandon the demand for democracy," ran one of the advertisement. "Keep up hope, don't retreat from the road of democracy."

Democracy movement leaders strongly criticised Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa, Beijing's appointee to run Hong Kong from July 1 after Britain withdraws, for calling on the population to abandon Tiananmen anniversary protests.
"We are allowed to hold commemorative activities as long as they are lawful," said legislator Cheung Man-kwong.
"I think Tung is alienating himself from the whole population," said Lee Cheuk-yan, a trade union leader, legislator and leader of a pro-democracy mass movement.

"He is putting himself in the place of the Chinese leadership and lecturing the people of Hong Kong, instead of siding with the rest of the population in their aspirations for a free China," Lee said.
The massacre brought one million Hong Kong sympathisers on to the streets in 1989.
